articles.title: How to nail an interview

body.support:
An interview is a talk where a boss sees if you'd be good at the job. For a first job, they want to see your **attitude**. Are you keen? Reliable? Friendly?

**Before.** Read the job ad again. Look up the business. Plan three stories from your life: working in a team, fixing a problem, being reliable.

**During.** Use **STAR** to tell a story:

- **Situation**: where you were.
- **Task**: what needed doing.
- **Action**: what **you** did.
- **Result**: what happened.

Smile. Look up. Speak clearly. Not sure what they mean? Ask!

At the end, ask them a question: *What training do new staff get?*

**After.** Send a short thank-you message.
body.core:
An interview is a short conversation where an employer works out if you'll be good at the job. For a first job, they're not expecting experience. They want to see your **attitude**: keen, reliable and friendly. Your job is to **show** it.

**Before.** Re-read the job ad, and look up the business: what it sells, who its customers are. Plan how you'll get there and arrive 10 minutes early. Then prepare **three stories** from your life: a time you worked in a **team**, a time you solved a **problem**, and a time you were **reliable**.

**During.** Most questions are about you, the job, or *a time when…*. Answer *a time when* questions with **STAR**:

- **Situation**: where you were. *At netball last season…*
- **Task**: what needed doing. *Our coach was sick for a game…*
- **Action**: what **you** did. This is the biggest part. *I organised the warm-up and the positions…*
- **Result**: what happened, or what you learnt. *We played well, and I learnt I can lead under pressure.*

Your **voice and body** matter too: a smile, eye contact, sitting up, speaking clearly. If you don't understand a question, it's fine to ask: *Sorry, do you mean…?* Be honest about your **availability**.

At the end, they'll usually ask, *Do you have any questions?* Always have one ready: *What would a normal shift look like?* or *What training do new staff get?*

**After.** Send a short **thank-you** message the same day. It's polite, and it reminds them of you.
body.extend:
A job interview is a structured spoken exchange. The employer tests whether your attitude, skills and availability fit the role. For entry-level jobs, they aren't mainly looking for experience. They want evidence of the right **attitude**: reliability, willingness to learn and good communication.

**Before.** Re-read the job ad's essential criteria, research the business, and plan your travel. Prepare **three stories** you can adapt: teamwork, problem-solving and reliability.

**During.** Behavioural questions (*Tell me about a time when…*) reward the **STAR** structure:

- **Situation**: brief context.
- **Task**: the goal or challenge.
- **Action**: your specific actions, the heart of the answer, in the first person.
- **Result**: the outcome, and ideally what you learnt.

Back up your claims. *I'm reliable* is just a claim. *I haven't missed a Saturday training session in three years* is evidence. Delivery matters too: posture, eye contact, pace and a warm, clear voice. If a question is unclear, ask. Clarifying is a strength. Be honest about availability.

Prepare questions of your own; they signal genuine interest.

**After.** A brief, prompt thank-you message reinforces a positive impression.

caseStudies.title: What employers really want

body.support:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** is a government group that studies jobs. In **2025**, it asked lots of employers about hiring young people.

What it found:

- More than half of employers had young people apply.
- **82%** of those employers hired at least one young person.
- **Six in ten** said they hired them because of their **attitude**.
- Not many said it was because of experience.

So attitude matters most! But you have to **show** it. Be on time. Smile. Listen. Tell real stories.
body.core:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** is a government agency. It studies jobs and skills. It surveys Australian employers. In **2025**, it shared what employers said about hiring young people aged **15 to 24**.

Here's what it found:

- **58%** of employers had young people apply for a job in the previous year.
- Of those employers, **82%** hired at least one young person.
- They were asked **why** they hired them. **Six in ten** said the young person had **the right attitude**.
- Far fewer said **experience** (19%) or **good communication** (18%).

So the top reason wasn't experience. It was attitude.

The catch: an interviewer can't see attitude unless you **show** it. Turn up early. Smile. Listen. Tell real stories about times you were reliable and worked hard. That's how they see and hear your attitude.
body.extend:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** is a federal government agency. It runs a regular survey of Australian employers about hiring. In **2025**, it published what employers said about applicants aged **15 to 24**.

- **58%** of employers reported having young applicants in the previous 12 months.
- Of those, **82%** hired at least one young person.
- Asked why, about **six in ten** said the young person had **the right attitude**. Far fewer named **relevant experience** (19%) or **good communication skills** (18%).

Many young jobseekers assume that having no experience rules them out. This data suggests otherwise. For many employers, attitude decides it.

But nobody can see attitude directly. Interviewers judge it from what you do: arriving on time, listening, showing interest. They also judge it from the evidence in your answers. That's why clear, specific examples matter. They turn a vague quality into something real.

teacher.overview: The boss level of Work Ready. Students prepare for a job interview: researching the job and business, planning three STAR stories (situation, task, action, result), substantiating claims with evidence, using voice and body well, clarifying questions and asking their own. The case study is Jobs and Skills Australia's 2025 research, where about six in ten employers who hired a young person said it was because of their attitude. The final task is a mock interview and a thank-you message.
prep: Line up interviewers: teachers, office staff, older students or (best) local employers. Five minutes each.
Print the question list and a simple feedback slip.
Decide how recordings will be made and stored.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Before
steps: **Hook (10 min):** ask a student, without warning, “Tell me about a time you worked in a team.” Then ask the class what would help.
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** before, during, after; STAR modelled on the netball answer.
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading.
**Annotate (10 min):** Anatomy of a STAR answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Stories
steps: **Prepare three stories (25 min).** Conference with students as they work.
**Case study (15 min):** what employers really want. Turn claims into evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Practise
steps: **Model (5 min):** you be interviewed by a student.
**Pair practice (30 min):** rotate interviewer and interviewee; use the question list.

steps: **Mock interviews (35 min):** with visiting interviewers if possible.
**Level Up, reflect (15 min):** review recordings; quick check; request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**STAR:** situation, task, action, result. **Three stories:** teamwork, solving a problem, being reliable. **Questions to ask (samples):** What does a normal shift look like? What training do new staff get?

**STAR answer:** 1 situation; 2 task; 3 action (the biggest part, in the first person); 4 result; 5 what I learnt; 6 link to the job.

**Sort:** “I'm just normal” — weak; Year 10, netball, keen — strong; “for the money” — weak; shopped here, friendly staff — strong; “No” — weak; normal shift question — strong.

**Case study:** the right attitude (about six in ten); show attitude by arriving early, smiling, listening, giving real examples, asking a question; evidence sample: *I've worked every Saturday at the market stall for a year without missing a day.*

realityCheck: **Nerves are the main barrier.** Practise in low-stakes pairs first, and let students choose who interviews them for the final.
**Visiting employers transform it.** Even two local managers for a lesson make the task real, and sometimes lead to actual jobs.

**Inappropriate questions.** Students should know some questions (about religion, family plans, ethnicity) shouldn't be asked; Youth Central's guide explains what to do. Mention it without scaring them.
**Cultural differences.** Eye contact and handshakes vary across cultures. Teach them as Australian workplace norms, not moral rules, and accept respectful alternatives.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the natural finale to Work Ready, using the job ad, the resume and workplace talk together.
